listings.name: Simon Fraser Red Leafs
listings.content: Represent Simon Fraser University in Burnaby. The Red Leafs sponsor teams in seven men's sports and nine women's sports. Notably, SFU is the only Canadian school that's a member of the U.S. NCAA, though they are in Division II, competing with mostly smaller, regional U.S. institutions. SFU no longer plays football, either American or Canadian; it had played under American rules in the NCAA, but logistical complications led the school to drop the sport after the 2022 season.

listings.name: UBC Thunderbirds
listings.content: Represent the University of British Columbia in the University Endowment Lands at the west edge of the Point Grey peninsula. The Thunderbirds field teams in 15 men's sports and 14 women's sports. Unlike SFU, UBC is a member of Canada's governing body for university sport, U Sports.

listings.name: Bill Reid Gallery of Northwest Coast Art
listings.content: The Gallery showcases the permanent collection of acclaimed Haida artist Bill Reid (1920–1998) and changing exhibitions of contemporary Northwest Coast Art. Gallery highlights include over 40 pieces of Bill Reid’s gold and silver jewelry, Reid’s bronze masterpiece Mythic Messengers, several of Reid’s works that were featured on the Canadian $20 bill and a full-scale totem pole, carved by James Hart of Haida Gwaii.

listings.name: Jack Poole Plaza
listings.content: Brick-paved plaza with good views of the North Shore mountains, Stanley Park and Coal Harbour. It is also the home of the Olympic Cauldron.

listings.name: Library Square and Vancouver Public Library
listings.content: The modern and attractive central branch of the City of Vancouver's Public Library is located in an architecturally interesting building, designed by Moshe Safdie. Constructed as a 'square within a circle', this building is reminiscent of a modern Roman Colosseum. Its design was chosen in a public competition. There are large public spaces around the building and a nice atrium space in the lobby. Guest internet access is available at VPL and visitors can also obtain guest wireless privileges from the library. If you prefer not to obtain a guest login, there are a few terminals that allow access to selected resources (bus schedules, government pages, etc.) without logging in.

listings.name: Robson Square
listings.content: Both an office building and public space designed by Vancouver architect Arthur Erikson, it houses the Provincial Courts and a satellite UBC campus. The building, which was built to represent a skyscraper on its side, is noted for its use of water and greenery and is mostly underground. The public space features a skating rink underneath Robson Street, which is the only outdoor rink in Vancouver.
listings.price: Skating is available during winter and is free, skate rentals are $3

listings.name: Vancouver Art Gallery
listings.content: You can see and learn a lot about Emily Carr in the permanent collection, but the rest of the gallery varies in quality depending on what they have been able to attract as special exhibits. Take advantage of admission by donation on Tuesday (5-9PM) and sample what is there before paying the full admission.

listings.name: Vancouver Lookout
listings.content: Located on the top floor of the Harbour Centre, the Lookout offers a full 360-degree panoramic view of the city from 130 m up. You'll see the downtown area, Stanley Park, the North Shore mountains and even the skyline of nearby Burnaby. The ticket is good for two trips during the day, so you can see it in the daytime and return for the sunset view.
listings.price: $18.25, discounts for children, seniors and students available; best prices if bought at Tourism Vancouver office

listings.name: Canada Place
listings.content: Built for Expo 86 as Canada's exhibit, today the building serves as a cruise ship terminal and the eastern building of Vancouver Convention Centre. It is also the site of an IMAX theatre and the luxurious Pan Pacific Hotel. Walk around the unique sailed structure and take in views of the building itself, Coal Harbour, and the North Shore. It uses white colour with a roof of funky "sails" or "waves", which is a curved triangular shape, that has made it a modern gem.

listings.name: Christ Church Cathedral
listings.content: Vancouver's oldest surviving church was completed in 1889. Often in the shadow of its neighbour, the 23-storey Cathedral Place, you should visit in the afternoon to see the sun shining through the stained glass windows.

listings.name: Marine Building
listings.content: This 22-storey Art Deco office tower was completed in 1930. Because of the Great Depression, only four floors were occupied for the first several years. Note the attention to detail on both the exterior, and in the lobby.

listings.name: Hotel Vancouver
listings.content: The third such hotel in this spot, the Hotel Vancouver was built over 11 years and completed in 1939. As with all Canadian Pacific hotels in Canada, the chateau-style is truly impressive. It was the tallest building in Vancouver until 1972. The hotel's first guests were King George and Queen Elizabeth. Bring binoculars for a close-up view of the building's many gargoyles.

listings.name: One Wall Centre
listings.content: Voted the world's best new skyscraper in 2001 by Emporis.

listings.name: Telus Garden
listings.content: Glass office building with a distinct outside that contains 4 storey gardens.

listings.name: Vancouver House
listings.content: A neo-futurist residential skyscraper with 49 floors. Its base is a triangle, that gradually changes into a rectangle - giving it a very uncanny/slim shape from some angles.

listings.name: Vancouver Opera
listings.content: Offers world-class performances from some of the world's best composers. The listed address is the ticket office, which is not in Vancouver's downtown. Most performances take place at Queen Elizabeth Theatre, which hosts a variety of entertainment performances in the downtown area.

listings.name: Vancouver Symphony Orchestra
listings.content: A great night out at reasonable prices. Students can purchase $10 tickets with the VSO Access Pass. Concerts generally take place at the Orpheum at the noted address.

listings.name: Long Table Distillery Ltd.
listings.content: A craft distillery of vodkas, gins, and other spirits, many of which bubble in the back room. Free tastings are offered on a 14-foot recovered-tree "long table" in the front room. If your only experience of gin and vodka comes from uninspiring mass-market pap, you are in for a treat. The friendly staff love explaining the finer points of which aromatics go in which chamber of their gleaming, copper 300-litre still. On Friday evenings 4-6PM, they park a food truck out front and hold a gin and tonic happy hour. Follow the buzz at #TGIGNT on Twitter.
On April 20th people congregate at the Vancouver Art Gallery to smoke marijuana and celebrate this unofficial holiday, a reflection of BC's relaxed attitudes towards cannabis.

listings.name: Canada Day at Canada Place
listings.content: A large, engaging, though somewhat corporate celebration of Canada's national holiday. The citizenship ceremony can be moving. There are usually several bands, fun activities for the kids, and exhibits of Canadian Forces and other bits of Canadiana.

listings.name: Canada Day Fireworks
listings.content: There is a fireworks display after dark on Canada Day.
listings.price: Free viewing from streets, premium Canada Place seating for a fee

listings.name: Vancouver Zombie Walk
listings.content: Usually either in the summer or near Halloween, anyone can choose to dress up and act as the living dead during this parade through Downtown. Although this has only been in Vancouver for about 2 years, thousands of people have already participated, and at least 500 people each year join in on this zombie walk. It is free, and mostly for plain fun, and is also an unofficial event. Each year, there is a set meeting spot. Everyone then walks throughout Downtown and up streets and parks all in one large group.

listings.name: Breka Bakery & Café
listings.content: Open 24/7 at all 7 locations, with 4 located downtown. Very large, very fresh selection of baked goods. All made locally, and then baked on site. Add-ons like oat, almond, soy milk and flavour shots are free. Limited selection of gluten-free and vegan options. All downtown locations are lively: limited seating during peak hours. Fanciest interior is at the newest location on Hastings St.

listings.name: Caffè Artigiano
listings.content: Excellent coffee shop featuring "latte art," but it's still great. IntelligentsiA coffee available. Great espresso. This small chain has a total of four locations in this district, plus other locations in the Lower Mainland and Calgary.

listings.name: Cartems Donuterie
listings.content: They modestly claim the title of "best donuts in Vancouver". They certainly have some of the most interesting flavours. Try the "whiskey bacon" donut. Also coffee and tea, served with a friendly smile in a hip setting.

listings.name: European Breads
listings.content: An organic crêpes café, which also sells various freshly-baked breads of organic wheat, rye, spelt, and other grains. Well set up for a light breakfast, lunch, or snack. Free wifi.

listings.name: Fritz Frie House
listings.content: This restaurant boasts what one of the best poutines in town. The curds are imported from Quebec. The garlic lover's mayo is fantastic too. Cleverly located next to the local Fitness World. $5 for a medium. Open until the wee hours in the morning, frequented by nightclubbers. Regularly wins local awards for fries.

listings.name: Japadog
listings.content: A Vancouver street food icon that now has its own shop. It's a twist on the traditional hot dog with your choice of pork, turkey or bratwurst smothered in Japanese flavours and toppings like seaweed, miso glaze, Japanese chilli and teriyaki sauce. There are also several Japadog carts around downtown, some with a kobe beef option. Look for the carts on Burrard St and in front of Waterfront Station.

listings.name: Mink, A Chocolate Café
listings.content: The coffee is strong, the hot chocolate is rich and the chocolate is plentiful. Dairy-free available. Waffles and fruit parfaits. The chocolate fondue with pound cake and seasonal fruit for dipping is excellent (just make sure there's at least two of you to share!). As a chocolate maker, they use their own chocolate in everything. Large selection of house-made chocolate bars, bonbons, & confections for retail.

listings.name: Pita Wrap Café
listings.content: The usual falafels, souvlakis, shawarmas and Greek plates, but very well executed.

listings.name: Tree's Organic Coffee & Roasting House
listings.content: A coffeehouse featuring carefully selected, 100% certified organic, coffee. Justifiably proud of its reaaaally good cheesecake. This is the flagship of a small local chain; there are other locations in Yaletown, Gastown and Richmond.

listings.name: Vancouver Community College Cafeteria
listings.content: The cafeteria is run by the culinary arts program so you get gourmet food at cafeteria prices. Usually have a large seafood selection. Don't miss the Asian Food program which has a separate service area. As you would expect from students, the quality can vary. However, it is hard to complain when you get a fancy meal for less than $8.

listings.name: Kamei Royal
listings.content: This is the Japanese restaurant to which you can bring your homesick Japanese business partners. Excellently prepared, professional-grade sushi, rice dishes, kushiyaki, and cooked-at-the-table sukiyaki. An authentic Japanese atmosphere, from the irasshaimase greeting to the pretty pictures in the bilingual menus to the serene decor. Tucked above a Tiffany's store on the second floor, you look out over the crowds on Georgia and Burrard, or inside at the chefs in the glass-walled kitchen. Another branch is on W Broadway in Kits.

listings.name: Medina Café
listings.content: Menu includes Moroccan-influenced dishes, fricasse (fried eggs with braised short ribs) and Belgian waffles with a choice of unusual sauces like milk chocolate lavender and white chocolate pistachio rosewater, plus many other breakfast and lunch concoctions. It seats about 75 or so, but lineups and long waits are still normal, especially for brunch on weekends.

listings.name: Shabusen Yakiniku House
listings.content: A Japanese and Korean BBQ House specializing in a large all-you-can-eat menu. Fun part of eating here is that you can order raw meat and cook it yourself on the grill installed at the table. There is another location in South Granville.

listings.name: Coast
listings.content: Fresh seafood from coastal regions throughout the world. Try the Chef's Community Table, where the chef prepares the food for up to 14 diners right at the table.

listings.name: Hy's Steakhouse & Cocktail Bar
listings.content: The most amazing service in Vancouver. Classy steakhouse that has been serving Vancouver for some fifty years. Charcoal steaks are the house specialty, but the menu also includes local cuisine like Pacific Salmon and Ahi Tuna. The servers do an incredible job and the food is excellent.

listings.name: Joe Forte's Seafood & Chop House
listings.content: Open daily for lunch and dinner; reservations strongly recommended. Usually mentioned amongst the top 5 restaurants in Vancouver, here you will find great food and great service. In the lavishly decorated open space, you may even catch a glimpse of a celebrity as you savour the oysters that are a specialty here.
listings.price: With glamour comes a price; expect to spend about $70/person for a complete dinner

listings.name: Miku
listings.content: Japanese restaurant that specializes in aburi (seared on the outside while raw inside). There's also a small bar at the entrance.

listings.name: Commodore Ballroom
listings.content: This is a large venue frequent location for live concerts. Has a large famous 'sprung' dance floor. Capacity is 900 people. On most nights, tickets are required to get in.

listings.name: The Railway Stage & Beer Cafe
listings.content: Popular bar that frequently features live music. The crowd is a mix of ages, although probably more over 30. It's not a big place, so it gets packed easily. There are more tables at the other end of the long bar if you want to sit down and talk.

listings.name: The Roxy
listings.content: Long-time Vancouver club which features top 40 rock. The house band, Loaded/Fully Loaded, covers some of the best of the recent pop and rock M-Sa, with country music on Sunday.

listings.name: Ambassador Hotel
listings.content: A boutique-style hotel with single, twin, double and queen rooms. Washrooms are shared (per floor) but are private upon entry.

listings.name: Cambie Hostel - Downtown
listings.price: Dorms start at $27, or $24 with Cambie Card

listings.name: SameSun Vancouver
listings.content: Hostel with modern amenities and decorated by bright splashes of colours on the wall.
listings.price: Dorms start at $35, private rooms at $85

listings.name: Best Western Plus Chateau Granville
listings.content: Rooms and suites with tea/coffee maker, microwave, and refrigerator. Exterior of building is unattractive, but rooms are pleasant. Surrounding area still in the process of being gentrified.

listings.name: The Burrard
listings.content: Old motor inn remodelled to go for the funky factor. Some of the rooms are small and its age still shows in spots, but there's lots of character, free wifi, new beds and mini-fridges and espresso machines in each room.

listings.name: Days Inn Vancouver Downtown
listings.content: It's an old building so some of the rooms are small and noisy. Otherwise, a typical Days Inn - clean, simple rooms, but not many extras. Free wireless Internet available.

listings.name: GEC Granville Hotel
listings.content: Mix of rooms with single queen, single king, two double beds or two queen beds.

listings.name: Kingston Hotel
listings.content: Single rooms have a 3/4 double bed and shared washroom facilities. Twin and double rooms have their own washrooms. Comes with a free continental breakfast.

listings.name: L'Hermitage
listings.content: Boutique-style hotel in a condo tower. Room options range from "Boutique" rooms that have a queen or king-size bed to one and two bedroom suites for extended stays. Amenities include a fitness room, heated outdoor saltwater pool and complementary wifi.

listings.name: Ramada Vancouver Hotel
listings.content: Accommodation includes full hot breakfast, adjacent fitness centre, business centre, guest laundry/dry cleaning service, 24-hr concierge, complimentary wifi and baggage storage. The hotel is pet-friendly and also has an on-site bar and lounge. Some rooms have kitchenettes.

listings.name: Victorian Hotel
listings.content: One of Vancouver's first guest houses, the hotel retains a lot of its original woodwork and Victorian-era details. Economy rooms have one or two beds and a sink, with a shared bathroom. Luxury rooms have one to three beds and full bathroom. There is complementary continental breakfast and wifi; secure parking is available for a fee.

listings.name: Atrium Hotel Vancouver
listings.content: Ideally located in Vancouver’s East Village, right across from the PNE, our hotel offers newly renovated, cozy rooms designed for comfort and value. Enjoy a complimentary breakfast and free parking, all just an 8-minute walk from the Coliseum—perfect for catching concerts and games. With quick, easy access to downtown, it's your affordable home base for exploring the city.

listings.name: Exchange Hotel Vancouver
listings.content: Opened in 2018 in the former stock exchange building.

listings.name: Fairmont Hotel Vancouver
listings.content: Vancouver's grand old hotel. Beautifully decorated and a firmly established part of Vancouver's history. The lounge is noted for its traditional afternoon tea.

listings.name: The Fairmont Waterfront
listings.content: A 5-star hotel with a stunning view wherever there's a window. Across from Canada Place.

listings.name: Hotel Le Soleil
listings.content: Suites and guestrooms with luxury touches like marble bathrooms and unique artwork and decor from local artisans and the Old World. Rated "One of the Top 100 Hotels in the World" - by Resorts & Great Hotels Magazine.

listings.name: Loden Hotel
listings.content: Has the modern look and feel with earthy tones, deep soaker tubs and a yoga studio. There's also a 24 hour fitness centre and free bike rentals. The floor to ceiling windows provide good harbour or city views (depending on which way your room faces).
listings.price: From $279. Additional fee for valet parking, internet access $15/day

listings.name: Marriott Pinnacle Downtown Hotel
listings.content: A good weddings and meetings hotel steps away from the harbour and cruise ship terminal. Fitness centre, indoor lap pool and whirlpool.

listings.name: The Metropolitan
listings.content: Luxury hotel featuring marble washrooms and soaker tubs.

listings.name: Pan Pacific Vancouver
listings.content: This modern hotel consists of an array of modern furnished luxury rooms and suites.

listings.name: Rosewood Hotel Georgia
listings.content: A historic Vancouver hotel where the rich and the royal have stayed in the past. Those guests have moved on but the hotel retains a mix of elegant rooms and suites. Amenities include a fitness centre and indoor saltwater pool.

listings.name: Shangri-La Hotel
listings.content: A luxury hotel located in the tallest building in Vancouver with 119 guest rooms, executive suites and space for meetings and events. Rooms include marble bathrooms, PVRs and floor to ceiling windows to take in the marvellous view. Other amenities include a 24 hour health club, outdoor pool and access to the Chi spa. The hotel also offers MARKET by Jean-Georges, Jean-Georges Vongerichten's Canadian debut.

listings.name: Sutton Place Hotel
listings.content: Classic-styled luxury hotel with spa, gym, concierge and the usual room amenities. Reviewers like the ambiance, the friendly staff and the location, but find the WiFi signal weak and thought some of the furnishings looked a bit dated.

listings.name: Wedgewood Hotel and Spa
listings.content: European-style boutique hotel listed on Conde Nast's gold list. The decor isn't modern but reviewers like the elegance and class of the hotel and found the rooms well appointed and comfortable. Amenities include a spa and fitness centre and business centre for internet access (no wifi in rooms).

listings.name: New Brighton Park
listings.content: Good-sized park tucked on the shore of the Burrard Inlet between port facilities. It provides an interesting, grittier view of the North Shore mountains with the port facilities and Second Narrows Bridge in sight. Amenities include playing fields, a children's playground, a beach and a trail along the shore. There is also the New Brighton Pool, a heated outdoor pool that is usually open from the Victoria Day long weekend to Labour Day (late May to early Sept).
listings.price: The park is free, $3-6 for the pool

listings.name: Hastings Racecourse
listings.content: Horse racing on most weekends.

listings.name: Momiji Garden
listings.content: Small Japanese garden built as an apology for Japanese internment.
listings.price: Free, except when the PNE is open during the second half of August

listings.name: East Van Cross
listings.content: This artwork installed in 2010, looks like a Christian cross, and is a reference is to the city’s Eastern half, which is traditionally less wealthy and harder-edged. Ironically almost half of Greater Vancouver residents identify as not having a religion, a fraction that is higher than any other large city in North America. This artwork is easily seen when looking south, while taking the SkyTrain Expo Line between Main Street-Science World station and Commercial-Broadway station. It is also a located a block east of VCC-Clark station on the SkyTrain Millenium Line.

listings.name: PNE
listings.content: Two week exhibition where extra rides and events are added to the usual Playland activities.

listings.name: Playland at the PNE
listings.content: Playland is a medium-sized amusement park, like something you may find at a U.S. county fair, and activities include a wooden rollercoaster, games, shows for kids and perhaps 20 or so other rides that spin, throw and hurl you in various ways.
listings.price: $20 if under 4 feet, $30 otherwise. Parents of kids under 12 pay $13

listings.name: Britannia Sushi
listings.content: This might be the best deal on sushi in the city. $4.95 for an 18 piece combo (including yam rolls) with miso soup, or teriyaki box. Decent quality and decor.

listings.name: Samurai Sushi on Fraser
listings.content: Well known for having huge portions for small prices. Take out available. There is another location at 1108 Davie in the West End, which is open until midnight.

listings.name: Bon's Off Broadway
listings.content: Bon's has a great atmosphere and excellent prices including $3 breakfast all day: 2 eggs, toast, bacon or sausage, and hashbrowns.

listings.name: La Casa Gelato
listings.content: This gelateria is a little off the beaten path, but the over 200 flavours will reward you!

listings.name: Ba Le
listings.content: A Vietnamese sandwich shop that is rather out of the way for most tourists but it regularly wins local awards for sandwiches and has delicious Vietnamese subs (including a vegetarian one) for less than $8.

listings.name: Red Wagon Cafe
listings.content: Small neighbourhood restaurant kind of like a country diner serving hearty portions of sandwiches, burgers and all day breakfast. It's probably best known for its pulled pork pancakes and sandwiches. Popular over lunch, so expect to wait for a table if arriving between noon and 1PM.

listings.name: Tacofino
listings.content: Taco chain that began in Tofino but now has locations all over Vancouver, the hastings branch offers a hip vibe and a large selection of craft-beer.
listings.price: $6 for a taco, $13 for a burrito

listings.name: Phnom Penh
listings.content: Authentic Cambodian restaurant which can attract large crowds.

listings.name: Cedar Cottage Neighbourhood Pub
listings.content: Upstairs is a funky little coffee house with lots of comfy seating, downstairs is a friendly pub, popular with a lot of local sports teams. There is a patio adjoining, with heat lamps for those cooler evenings. Friday nights are almost always packed.

listings.name: Odd Society Spirits
listings.content: Microdistillery with their own cocktails. They offer a tasting with a sample of each of their different liquors as well as small tours.

listings.name: St. Augustine's Pub
listings.content: A pub that takes its beer seriously. The two page beer menu features craft beers from across Canada and U.S. and there are live reports on how full each keg is. The food choices are pretty standard for a pub — burgers, sandwiches, pizza and finger foods — but it's well done. There are also a number of TVs for catching the game.

listings.name: Bomber Brewing
listings.content: Microbrewery that offers flights, snacks and sells canned 6-packs of some of their beers. Offers small tours too.

listings.name: Parallel 49 Brewing
listings.content: Microbrewery.

listings.name: Powell Street Craft Brewery
listings.content: Microbrewery that offers flights, snacks and growler fills.

listings.name: Storm Brewing
listings.content: Oldest microbrewery in Vancouver. They don't offer flights, but will give you tastings of anything one at a time for free (small donation suggested).

listings.name: Off the Rail Brewing
listings.content: Microbrewery with a large number of beers and some snacks. They've begun offering pint cans of some of their beers and offer growler fills.

listings.name: Atrium Inn
listings.content: Standard motel room with wireless internet in each room and a complimentary continental breakfast. Located on a busy street so traffic noise can sometimes be a problem. Will provide complimentary shuttle service to downtown and some nearby attractions (although space is limited).
listings.price: $150 and up, suites start around $240 (summer rates)

listings.name: The Waldorf Hotel
listings.content: The Waldorf is a creative hub in the heart of East Vancouver where contemporary art, music, food and culture convene under one roof. The programming for the space will be both artistically expansive and thematically inclusive. The complex consists of thirty rooms, two restaurants (Nuba Cafe and The Leeteg Dining Room), a Tiki bar (restored and retrofitted with a vintage analogue audiophile sound system), a hair salon (run by Barbarella Hair), a gift shop, a nightclub and a live music venue. In the works are a multi-media theatre space and recording studio (tied to a residency program for visiting musicians).The Waldorf joins a new wave of Vancouver businesses that are conversing with the city, setting a benchmark for culture and hospitality.

listings.name: Gastown
listings.content: The oldest part of downtown. You will find cobble-paved boulevards and over-priced tourist traps selling every imaginable thing you can print "Vancouver" on. Popular with tourists are the Gastown Steam Clock, promoted as the only active steam clock in the world but in fact an electric clock that pumps steam, rather an underwhelming experience. The area is notorious for aggressive beggars-drug addicts who are quite unsettling.

listings.name: Dominion Building
listings.content: A distinctive red and mustard coloured building completed in 1910. It was the first steel-framed high-rise built in Vancouver and briefly was the tallest commercial building in the British Empire.

listings.name: Chinatown Millennium Gate
listings.content: Located at the western edge of Chinatown, it consists of ornamental arches with tiled roofs in traditional Chinese style.

listings.name: Dr. Sun Yat-Sen Classical Chinese Garden
listings.content: A Ming-dynasty style garden in Chinatown. Built in 1986 by Chinese craftsmen using traditional materials, tools, and techniques, this was the first classical garden built outside China. The gardens combine traditional Chinese buildings, plants, a small lake, and curved footpaths to create the illusion of a very big place within a single block. Tours are available. Compared to the city park next door, the differences are quiet but profound: more interesting materials, richer vistas, greater serenity.

listings.name: Dr. Sun Yat-Sen Park
listings.content: Constructed by Vancouver-area designers at the same time as its classical garden neighbour, this public park shares the lake and the Chinese garden look. But this is a city park, and free to enter.

listings.name: Gastown Steam Clock
listings.content: A clock that tries to look old and belches steam every 15 minutes may not be the most stunning landmark, but it has an endearing charm in a kitschy kind of way. It was built to take advantage of the steam vents that are all over downtown Vancouver, but it never lived up to its billing and now relies on electricity to count the minutes. It is one of a kind though and remains a photographic pilgrimage for thousands of Vancouver tourists.

listings.name: Sam Kee Building
listings.content: This two-storey building is the world's narrowest commercial building according to the Guinness Book of World Records, with a width of just 4'11" (1.5 m) at its base. Its slim size is due to the city expropriating most of the lot to widen the street. The owner went ahead and built anyway, and businesses have been operating out of its confines since 1913. If you do take a look, the perspective is better from the other (north) side of Pender.

listings.name: Sun Tower
listings.content: A high-rise building built in the Beaux-Arts style. It was completed in 1912 and was the tallest building in the British Empire at the time. The tower is noted for its dome (painted to look like copper cladding) and its exterior was used in the TV series, Smallville.

listings.name: Vancouver Police Museum
listings.content: Exhibits on the history of Vancouver's police, unusual weapons that have been confiscated and notable Vancouver crimes. There are also a number of programs and activities geared towards kids.

listings.name: Victory Square
listings.content: A small park covering one city block. It has the cenotaph commemorating the dead from World War I and is the site of Vancouver's Remembrance Day ceremonies.

listings.name: Chinese New Year
listings.content: Because there is such a strong Chinese population in the city, the Lunar New Year period is often one of the most exciting and colourful in the city. There is usually a parade in Chinatown and many of the public schools usually have a day off on Chinese New Year. You can also catch celebrations at Tinseltown mall (1 minute from Stadium Skytrain station), and in Richmond at the International Buddhist Temple. There, visitors can experience Chinese New Year festivities with traditional snacks and foods, auspicious flower arrangements, Chinese calligraphy and exciting raffles.

listings.name: Meat & Bread
listings.content: Simple menu but good food. There are four sandwiches, mostly focusing on roasted or braised meat (the Porchetta is the signature sandwich), and two sides that change daily. The bread is pretty dense but the portion of meat is generous so it's a filling meal. To finish it off (if you have room), you can get a bowl of Maple Bacon ice cream. The ambiance is interesting as well, with a couple of long tables for seating... in case you want to chat with your neighbours while chowing down your sandwich.

listings.name: Old Spaghetti Factory
listings.content: Spaghetti and other standard Italian dishes, but well-priced and has sidewalk seating.

listings.name: Phnom Penh
listings.content: Very popular restaurant tucked away on a side street in Chinatown that has been winning local readers choice awards for 20 years. The menu is Vietnamese and Cambodian with a large number of dishes. The deep-fried chicken wings and butter beef (similar to beef carpaccio but slightly more cooked, with soy sauce and cilantro) are both very tasty and amongst the most popular dishes. Portions are a good size and in line with the price. It gets crowded quickly, so expect to wait if arriving after 5PM most nights.

listings.name: Save On Meats
listings.content: Diner-style restaurant that does simple comfort food well. Breakfast menu includes three egg omelettes and eggs benedict; lunch/dinner menu has sandwiches, some entrees and possibly the best burger value in Vancouver (bacon and cheeseburger with fries for $7). Full breakfast menu is served until 11AM on weekdays and 4PM on weekends. Eggs are available all day.

listings.name: Steamworks
listings.content: Long-standing brew pub that is popular with locals and tourists. There's a patio and restaurant at street level; pool tables and bar downstairs. The menu is extensive with pub standards like burgers and nachos, but also includes steaks, seafood and pasta.

listings.name: The Irish Heather
listings.content: Nice atmosphere, excellent pheasant, and apparently the only place in Vancouver that serves real Guinness.

listings.name: Waffleland Café
listings.content: Delicious Belgian and Norwegian style waffles, sweet and savoury. Excellent vegetarian and vegan options.
listings.image: Vegan chicken n' waffle at Waffleland.jpg

listings.name: Al Porto
listings.content: Nice Mediterranean-themed decor with a variety of pizza, pasta, seafood and meat dishes.

listings.name: Chambar
listings.content: Belgian restaurant with mussels and a variety of meat dishes on the menu. A small but delicious selection of vegetarian options. The beer list includes over 25 beers from Belgium. Wide selection of wines. Save room for the fascinating desserts. Don't be surprised if the general manager is the one who takes your empty plates; they are that involved. Exquisite food plus excellent service equals one of the best dining experiences in the city.

listings.name: Water Street Cafe
listings.content: Elegant restaurant known for its pasta and seafood dishes.

listings.name: Wildebeest
listings.content: A restaurant with some unique menu items that draw rave reviews from many but claims of being overhyped from others. The menu is meat-centric with dishes from varying parts of the animal — think pork jowls with oats, bone marrow, beef cheeks, as well as more traditional cuts like rib eye and roast chicken breasts. The restaurant makes good use of its Gastown location with brick walls and wooden tables and follows current trends with a long table so you can get to know your fellow diners. Plates are meant to be shared and some reviewers feel they are small, particularly for the price. There is a wine bar downstairs and the cocktail menu has some creative and tasty mixes.
listings.price: Plates range from $3-42, with most between $10-20

listings.name: Guilt and Company
listings.content: Creative and artsy sort of bar. Features some unique beers on tap and a selection of board games; order cheese from the bar and play some giant Jenga. Often features indie rock performances.

listings.name: Lamplighter
listings.content: One part sports bar and one part club gives this bar a dual personality which works for some and not for others. The crowd is a more mixed and mellow than Shine or Fabric.

listings.name: MIA Nightclub
listings.content: Smallish dance club with a variety of music, depending on the night.

listings.name: The Alibi Room
listings.content: Offers an array of microbrews with an emphasis on British Columbia breweries, as well as a diverse food menu.

listings.name: The Black Frog
listings.content: Smallish pub with some character. Good spot for pre-activity drinks or if you want somewhere not as loud. Also has a small but well prepared selection of burgers, sandwiches and fish and chips that are an excellent value.

listings.name: The Blarney Stone
listings.content: Bit of an Irish bar, bit of a dance club. Attracts a 20-something crowd most nights. Irish showband Killarney are a regular feature.

listings.name: The Cambie
listings.content: Frontier-looking unpretentious bar with well-worn wooden benches and tables. Popular with the younger crowd and the nearby backpackers hostel. Lots of rock music and no dance floor. Pitchers are amongst the cheapest in Vancouver.

listings.name: Columbia Hotel
listings.content: Hostel accommodations in an old historical building in the middle of Gastown.

listings.name: Patricia Hotel
listings.content: Very basic hotel that is a good option if you want something cheap and don't mind a small room in a bad part of town. The rooms are tidy and come with small TVs and private bathrooms. Wifi is available but signal strength varies. Room options range from Budget and Basic rooms with one double bed to Quad Rooms with two queen beds and views of the city. There is a pub on the ground floor that sometimes has live music.

listings.name: St Clair Hotel Hostel
listings.content: The hotel-hostel is a heritage-listed building, built-in 1911 by Captain Henry Pybus and architect Samuel Birds. It was the first concrete building in Vancouver, and was built as accommodation for railway and ocean-going passengers from both Pacific and Atlantic locations. The nautical theme has been preserved.

listings.name: H.R. MacMillan Space Centre and Planetarium
listings.content: The Space Centre is not unlike Science World, with most activities fascinating primarily to pre-teens. The planetarium, however, is a more interesting excursion, and will not be so fascinating to children. It is a small planetarium staffed by volunteers whose knowledge of all things space will stun and amaze you.

listings.name: Museum of Vancouver
listings.content: The largest civic museum in Canada, with over 1 million items from Vancouver's history, only a fraction of which fit in the exhibit halls. Tucked away to the left off the Orientation Gallery is a series of rooms telling Vancouver's story from the 19th century to the 1970s. The museum makes an effort to tell many stories of Vancouver: English Canadian, First Nations, various immigrant groups, etc. Kid-friendly exhibits.
listings.price: $20, senior or student $15, youth (6 to 17) $15, children (5 and under) free

listings.name: Vancouver Maritime Museum
listings.content: Canada's premiere western maritime museum. Covers the maritime history of Canada, includes artifacts, models and the St. Roch ship. The museum apparently has far more things than space to show them, so they frequently rotate their exhibitions in fascinating thematic arrangements. Previous exhibitions included such familiar topics as the history of the Vikings, to the less familiar "1500 years of Croatian sailors". Check for $2 discount coupons that you can print from the website.
listings.price: (credit card only) Adult $13.50, senior or student $11, youth (ages 6-18) $10, child 5 and under free, Family Pass (2 adults and 4 children) $38

listings.name: Vanier Park
listings.content: Surrounds the Kits Peninsula, with trails for joggers and bikers paralleling it, and some green grass and trees. This unique location is famous as an ideal place flying kites and hosts a Kite Flying Festival every summer. Stunning views of English Bay, Stanley Park, and downtown.

listings.name: Kitsilano Beach
listings.content: It's the sandy beach for the young to hang out and be seen at. Kits beach also features beach volleyball courts and a large public swimming pool. Popular in the summer, the salt water pool is 137.5 m in length and runs along the ocean's edge.

listings.name: Reckless Bike Stores
listings.content: Bicycle rentals and sales.
listings.price: $23.50 for 2 hr, $38.50 for half day, $54.50 for 24 hours. Tandem bikes, trailers and baby seats extra charge

listings.name: Cooper Boating
listings.content: Sailboat Racing. Offers drop-in Friday night racing for all comers. No skill or knowledge is required, in fact the sailing is strictly novice level.
listings.price: $25, with an additional $15 membership fee (which is valid for 2 years)

listings.name: Stanley Industrial Alliance Stage
listings.content: The main stage for the Vancouver Arts Theatre Company. Mostly shows Broadway musicals and other large theatre productions.

listings.name: Vancouver Arts Club Theatre
listings.content: The Granville Island stage for the Vancouver Arts Club Theatre Company.

listings.name: The Improv Centre
listings.content: Long-running improv company in the Improv Centre on Granville Island.

listings.name: Bard on the Beach Shakespeare Festival
listings.content: Annual summer Shakespeare festival held in tents. Each year there are two mainstage productions and two productions for the smaller stage. Even if you have tickets, plan to line up at least an hour before the show to get good seats. Many people will bring a picnic lunch/dinner (purchased at nearby Granville Island) to enjoy while they wait to be admitted.

listings.name: Greek Day
listings.content: Greek Day is a family-oriented street festival that invites visitors to taste Greek food at its many kiosks while enjoying entertainment and activities for all ages. It is the culmination of the Hellenic Heritage Month that celebrates Greek heritage and culture. Greek Day takes place on the last Sunday of every June along West Broadway between Macdonald St and Blenheim St.

listings.name: KitsTreeMap
listings.content: Vancouver, apart from the mountains and the ocean, is famous for its variety of trees, tree-lined streets and cherry blossoms in the spring. No area more so typifies this veritable tree heaven than Kitsilano. Walk down most of the streets in the neighbourhood and you will find yourself beneath one stunning canopy after another. As well as street plantings of the same species of tree, there are hundreds of different individual trees in front gardens, alleyways and public places. One of the most famous tree avenues in Vancouver is the Tulip trees on 10th Ave from Blenheim to Dunbar.

listings.name: Vancouver Folk Festival
listings.content: A truly amazing folk festival featuring spectacular views of the harbour and mountains. The Vancouver Folk Festival typically features several stages, and a wonderous mix of traditional and contemporary artists.

listings.name: Vancouver Fringe Festival
listings.content: Every year, close to 100 theatre groups and performers from across Canada and around the world perform for 11 days in diverse venues, from theatres to garages to a moving Aquabus.

listings.name: Whole Foods
listings.content: High-end organic grocery store featuring a veggie buffet take away or eat in. Also has a Robson Street location downtown.

listings.name: Cheesecake, etc.
listings.content: Vancouver's first late-night dessert cafe. Opened in 1979, it is an authentic Vancouver cultural experience. Featuring the original "Vancouver-style", it is a light cheesecake with various toppings added.

listings.name: East is East
listings.content: An interesting concept that sometimes works with low shared tables and wailing Asian music in a carpeted room. Decent chai to go with Indian/Tibetan/Pakistani/Iranian food. Some say service is lacking and portions are small.

listings.name: The Naam
listings.content: Vegetarian restaurant with organic options. Food taken from numerous cooking styles. Some love the Naam, some are disappointed by food, service and cleanliness. Wine and beer available.

listings.name: Aphrodite's Cafe and Pie Shop
listings.content: A friendly cafe that uses locally-grown and organic ingredients with a first-class menu that's long on vegetarian and vegan dishes. The brunch on Saturday and Sunday is delicious or try the pie and chai combination. Service is sometimes slow, so expect a wait, particularly when crowded. Lunch and dinner on weekdays; no reservations. Pies to go can be purchased at the pie shop next door.

listings.name: Banana Leaf
listings.content: Malaysian food is a vibrant mingling of Chinese, Indian, Thai, Indonesian, and Malay, and it springs to life at Banana Leaf with rich flavours beautifully presented, yet in an efficient, low-key atmosphere. Many dishes can be prepared vegetarian. Other locations are on West Broadway (Mt Pleasant), Davie, Robson, and Denman.

listings.name: Heirloom Vegetarian
listings.content: A bright, airy, colourful space and an all-vegetarian menu with extensive vegan choices. They favour local and fair-trade ingredients. There is brunch menu F-Su 9AM-4PM (weekends).

listings.name: The Eatery
listings.content: A fusion Japanese restaurant. The food is anything Japanese with a North American twist to it. The crowd can best be described as your usual 20-something crowd. Be prepared for kitsch overload.

listings.name: Tojo's
listings.content: Serves innovative Japanese cuisine. Try the omakase menu, where you leave the details of your 5-course meal to the chef's discretion. The vegetarian omakase can have spectacularly realistic-looking sushi made from vegetables. À la carte menu also available — but why skip the chance to let the master delight you? Winner of the "Best Japanese Restaurant" awards from Vancouver Magazine every year since 1991.

listings.name: Vij's
listings.content: Indian restaurant that combines Indian spices and cooking techniques with local ingredients. New York Times food writer Mark Bittman said that Vij’s was: "Easily among the finest Indian restaurants in the world."

listings.name: Afghan Horsemen
listings.content: The exotic decor and rich flavours justify this restaurant's pride in Afghan culture and cuisine. Try one of the platters for two people ($54-76). Numerous vegetarian options, and some vegan dishes too. Try to stay for the mesmerizing belly-dancer's performance.

listings.name: Go Fish
listings.content: Some of the best fish and chips in Vancouver, along with seasonal fish-based dishes all using fresh ingredients from local fishers. It's just a shack with some outdoor seating and may be a little hard to find; easiest to reach by foot or by bike. Look up driving directions if going by car – the route is not straightforward.

listings.name: Sandbar
listings.content: Enjoy a variety of fish and seafood while looking out over Granville Island and False Creek. Also has a number of tapas and meat dishes.

listings.name: Darby's Pub
listings.content: A local favourite, Darby’s is one of Kitsilano’s oldest neighbourhood pubs and has the best rooftop patio in the neighbourhood. Featuring live entertainment, comedy & karaoke nights, UFC, all broadcast & PPV Canucks games. With a classic pub menu focusing on quality.

listings.name: Granville Island Brewing Company
listings.content: Visit this local brewery and sample their brews in their taproom. Taster sleeves and full pints of this locally brewed beer.

listings.name: The Wolf and Hound
listings.content: Irish-themed pub with a good selection of draft beers and live music.

listings.name: Backstage Lounge
listings.content: Drinks and pub eats with live music most nights. Has a good selection of domestic and imported beers on tap, with nightly drink specials.

listings.name: Granville Island Hotel
listings.content: The only accommodation on Granville Island. Some of the standard rooms have a water view plus there are six executive suites and two penthouse suites. All rooms come with wireless and high-speed internet and there is a jacuzzi room on site.

listings.name: Queen Elizabeth Park
listings.content: An old quarry that was converted into a number of gardens and ponds. The top of the park is the highest point in the city of Vancouver and offers views of the entire city.

listings.name: Bloedel Conservatory
listings.content: Tropical plants and birds under the white dome.

listings.name: Vancouver City Hall
listings.content: Built on the rise over False Creek, the building has nice grounds and provides a different view into downtown Vancouver and the mountains behind.

listings.name: Vancouver Canadians
listings.content: Vancouver's minor league (single A) baseball team.

listings.name: Hawker's Delight
listings.content: At Main and King Edward Hawker's servers up authentic Malaysian/Singaporean dishes at $4-5. Fast-paced atmosphere (as the name would suggest). Good vegetarian options.

listings.name: Heartwood Community Cafe
listings.content: Successor to the popular Rhizome Cafe, serves bistro food, organic coffee, and alcoholic drinks. They seek to build community, and offer a meeting room for events.

listings.name: Lucy's Eastside Diner
listings.content: A slightly self-conscious reinvention of the classic burgers-and-pancakes diner. Being open all night long is good. Breakfast 24 hours a day is even better. The friendly and flexible service is great. The milkshakes laced with whisky, rum, and on request, bacon? Priceless. Good range of vegetarian selections. Since there aren't many all-night restaurants, Lucy's can get crowded late at night after clubs close.

listings.name: Vera's Burger Shack
listings.content: One of a local chain, well known for tasty, made-to-order hamburgers and a casual atmosphere. Vegetarian options and beer also served. Take-out also.

listings.name: The Acorn
listings.content: Opened in 2012, this is one of Vancouver's few restaurants to offer high cuisine that is entirely vegetarian, with many vegan and gluten-free options. Open for dinner every night and for weekend brunch. Their bar also serves creative and tasty cocktails. No reservations taken, and veggie foodies have few other options, so expect a wait unless you come soon after they open.

listings.name: Shiro Sushi
listings.content: If Toshi is too busy, walking west a half dozen blocks will bring you to another affordable family-run sushi restaurant with friendly service and a packet of Pocky with your bill.

listings.name: Sun Sui Wah Seafood Restaurant
listings.content: An excellent Chinese restaurant, the chefs are excellent cooks. Beware there are long lineups and reservations are a must.

listings.name: Toshi Sushi
listings.content: A small mostly family-run sushi restaurant that serves relatively cheap, good sushi. Avoid the garlic beef, but one must try the tempura. It's a popular spot so it's best to get there before 5PM.

listings.name: Locus Restaurant
listings.content: Local favourite with a variety of dishes that incorporate local and seasonal ingredients. Will substitute tofu for meat if requested.

listings.name: Seasons in the Park
listings.content: If the weather is nice, this restaurant has one of the best views in the city since it is the highest point in Vancouver. Surprisingly, for a restaurant with this good a location, the food and service are excellent and the prices are reasonable. Try the rack of lamb and the stuffed mushrooms. Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin ate here when they had their 1994 summit in Vancouver.
listings.price: Mains run from $17 to $34. Appetizers from $7 to $13
listings.address: 405 West 33rd Ave (at the top of Queen Elizabeth Park)

listings.name: Douglas Guest House
listings.content: Victorian house converted to B&B. Reviewers indicated the hearty breakfasts are good and the location is convenient but a couple of the rooms could be cleaner. Owned by the same owner as the Windsor House.

listings.name: Windsor Guest House
listings.content: Victorian house converted to B&B. Reviewers indicated the hearty breakfasts are good and the location is convenient but a couple of the rooms could be cleaner. Owned by the same owner as the Douglas House.

listings.name: Holiday Inn - Vancouver Centre
listings.content: Clean rooms and courteous service, although the decor could be updated.
listings.price: $160–250 in summer, cheaper rates at other times

listings.name: Park Inn & Suites
listings.content: Mix of rooms ranging from a standard hotel room to kitchenette to suites. Some rooms have views of downtown and the mountains. High-speed internet and fitness centre on site.
listings.price: $160–300 in summer, cheaper rates at other times

listings.name: VanDusen Botanical Garden
listings.content: VanDusen Botanical Garden has a very large collection of plants in the outdoor gardens. Especially interesting are the Canadian ecosystems, with samples of prairie and deep woods fauna. On the last weekend in April, the garden has a giant plant sale with many species from all over the world (they don't always have a Canadian official there to grant export, however). Plant seeds are available in the gift shop.

listings.name: Jewish Museum and Archives of BC
listings.content: A small museum that documents the history of the Jewish community in British Columbia. Check for interesting summer programs and tours at this museum; in 2007 it operated a "Tour de Blintz" cycling tour, which took participants to local Jewish eateries.

listings.name: Vancouver Holocaust Education Centre
listings.content: A teaching museum that focuses on the Holocaust, genocide, and anti-racism education. The museum has small thought-provoking temporary exhibits, but these may not be on display during the summer months when the museum traditionally works on mounting its next exhibit.

listings.name: Fraser River Park
listings.content: This is a local secret that has spectacular views of the airport. One can watch the planes come and go across the river. This park is popular for dog lovers, as its secluded location is perfect for letting dogs roam free. The park is large enough to have a big field for picnics and games, while the riverfront area has its own beach, depending on the tides. At the edge of the park is an industrial park and a golf course.

listings.name: All India Sweets
listings.content: Excellent vegetarian all you can eat Indian food buffet for $9.95.

listings.name: Samurai Sushi House
listings.content: Well known for having huge portions for small prices. It also has fresher sushi than some more expensive places. During meal times, it can be very difficult to get a seat. In the summer, it can be nice to get take out and walk down to Columbia Park (1 block east, ~5min). Be sure to try their toro (fatty tuna), and salmon sushi/sashimi. Stay away from their tuna sushi/sashimi because it tends to be too frozen. There is another location at 1108 Davie in the West End.

listings.name: 2400 Motel
listings.content: Older motel with a number of bungalow units. Reviewers indicate rooms can be small, but they are clean and quiet with a certain charm lent by their age.

listings.name: A Vancouver Traveller Bed and Breakfast
listings.content: Three rooms in a renovated old home in residential area. North Suite has a minimum stay of three nights, other rooms require two nights minimum June-Sept.

listings.name: Days Inn Vancouver Metro
listings.content: Reviews indicate the rooms can be small but the beds are comfortable.

listings.name: Granville House B&B
listings.content: B&B in a newer Tudor revival style house. Each room has a king size bed and internet connection.

listings.name: Coast Vancouver Airport Hotel
listings.content: The only hotel near the airport within the City of Vancouver.

listings.name: Irving K. Barber Learning Centre
listings.content: This library has the Automated Storage and Retrieval System (ASRS), an automated "robot librarian" cranes scurry along 5-story shelves holding 1.6 million books, at the beck and call of human librarians. For a geek thrill, watch them through the ground floor windows on the north side of the building. On the 2nd floor, near the Circulation desk, is a more limited view.

listings.name: Beaty Biodiversity Museum
listings.content: Home to Canada's largest blue whale skeleton, a herbarium, and a wide array of animal specimens including fish, insects, arthropods, tetrapods, marine invertebrates and fossils.

listings.name: Chan Centre for the Performing Arts
listings.content: A concert hall and events centre; often the location of convocation ceremonies.

listings.name: Morris and Helen Belkin Art Gallery
listings.content: A small gallery with regular exhibitions. What looks like a woodpile outside is actually a sculpture, made of concrete.

listings.name: Nitobe Memorial Garden
listings.content: One of the most traditional, authentic Japanese gardens in North America and among the top five Japanese gardens outside of Japan.

listings.name: UBC Botanical Garden
listings.content: Canada's longest continuously operating university garden, it contains over 8000 different kinds of plants in both designed landscapes and coastal forest settings. Must-sees are the Asian garden, the alpine garden and the food garden. An enchanting oasis. Compared to the more-visited Van Dusen Botanical Garden, the remoteness of the garden means fewer people and a quieter, more private setting. Guided tours free with advance notice.
listings.price: $7 (discounts available), audioguide $3. Free for UBC students, and faculty, staff, or neighbours holding a Garden Pass

listings.name: UBC Museum of Anthropology
listings.content: Devoted to world cultures, but with an emphasis on the First Nations of the Northwest Coast. Includes a splendid collection of totem poles, a mind-boggling array of artifacts from around the world, and a number of changing exhibits.
listings.price: $15.68 adults, $13.44 students/seniors, children 6 and under free ($7.84 flat rate Tu 5-9PM)

listings.name: Jericho Beach
listings.content: Is a more family oriented sandy beach with a large picnicking area. The beach forms a crescent shape which creates a sheltered swimming area that is relatively shallow. In the summer, the beach is patrolled by lifeguards who monitor beach near the floating dock. Jericho Beach is also a great location to go windsurfing or dinghy sailing.

listings.name: Spanish Banks
listings.content: Is a set of three sandy beaches further west towards UBC. When the tide is out you can walk way out on the mudflats. This is a popular spot for skimboarders and kiteboarders. The area has a large stretch of beach which makes for a popular beach volleyball area as well as a scenic multi-pathway system, connecting Jericho Beach to UBC, making a fine running or cycling course. A large field behind the beach has been designated as an off-leash area for dogs and part of the beach as well.

listings.name: Wreck Beach
listings.content: Probably North America's most famous and busiest clothing optional beach. It is a sandy beach. The trail to Wreck beach is near the West Parkade, or more precisely at the extreme west end of University Boulevard just past the Place Vanier residences. You can either park on Marine Drive or you can take transit to UBC and continue down the same road the bus brought you on foot. The steep stairs are not recommended for the faint of heart. There is always a festive atmosphere at this beach and many types of goods are for sale from jewellery, to food, to beer. Watch out as the police do occasionally crack down on drug use and open consumption of alcohol.

listings.name: Pacific Spirit Regional Park
listings.content: A mostly inland park almost entirely covered with forests. It separates the University of British Columbia on the west from urban areas of Vancouver on the east. It has 55 km of hiking trails crossing through the park, of which around 30 km of trails that can be used for cycling and around 30 km can be used as equestrian trails. While It is a significantly larger park than Stanley Park, and is well used by those wanting a workout, do not expect to find any crowds like at Stanley Park.

listings.name: University Village
listings.content: It has a full-service Starbucks Coffee as well as a Blenz, Omio Japanese Restaurant, Pita Pit, McDonald's, and a number of smaller cafes etc. An underground food court has about nine Chinese, Japanese, Indian and Persian buffets, with lunch or dinner. See listing under "Buy" for further information.

listings.name: AMS Student Nest
listings.content: The Nest is UBC's student union building. Within the Nest, there are a number restaurants and fast food outlets.

listings.name: Gold Train Express
listings.content: This rather misleadingly-named restaurant actually serves Vietnamese food, including a very good pho (beef with rice noodles).

listings.name: Koerners Pub
listings.content: Pub run by the Graduate Student Society. Has a patio, free pool, shuffleboard, and foosball. "Mellow Monday" open mic nights.

listings.name: The Pit
listings.content: A bar with a dance floor, run by the student society and famously first proposed by David Suzuki. Student ID required for Wednesday "Pit Nights" which are always packed. Inexpensive pub food served in the Burger Bar.

listings.name: The Gallery Lounge
listings.content: A smallish student-run pub, the Gallery is usually quieter than the Pit, and is a good place to go to grab a pint after class - and closer than Koerner's. Karaoke nights on Tuesday are a hoot, also open mic nights on Mondays and DJ nights on Fridays.

listings.name: Pacific Spirit Hostel at UBC
listings.content: Private or twin rooms with shared washroom and kitchen facilities. Open from mid-May to mid-August.

listings.name: Gage Towers
listings.content: Low-rise complex with a range of rooms. One bedroom and studio suites have private washroom and kitchenette. A tower suite room provides a private bedroom with a shared washroom and kitchenette (between 4-6 people). Open from mid-May to mid-August.

listings.name: West Coast Suites
listings.content: One bedroom suites with kitchenettes. Open year round.

listings.name: HI Vancouver-Jericho Beach
listings.content: Open 24 hr May 1 - Sep 30. Located 100 m from the beach and between UBC campus and downtown. Beautiful and quiet park setting but the 20-25min bus ride downtown leaves some feeling isolated.
listings.price: $18-22 for a bed in the dorm
